plan:
## Pitch

**Brand strategist: The 12:40 Call**
Start with the angriest person in this story: the patient whose call rings out at lunch.
The first screen shows a phone ringing out. Nothing else.
Then the owner fills in their numbers. Each field has its label printed above the box.
The result is three bars at 6, 12 and 24 months: hire a receptionist, add an answering tool, or change nothing.
I want the "change nothing" bar to be the tallest one on the page.
If I can't sketch it on a napkin in four boxes, it isn't ready.

**Luthier: Before the Ring, After the Ring**
Before the owner opens this page, they are looking at the missed-call log on the front desk phone.
After it, they forward the result to the practice manager, or they close the tab.
So the first input copies the log: "Missed calls last week."
The last thing on the page is a one-line summary they can paste into an email.
One word needs pinning down first. "Workload" means calls per week. It does not mean hours.
Labels sit above every box, in 16px type, and they stay visible while the user types.

**Clinic owner (buyer; voxxy): Who Picks Up**
Last spring a mum rang us three times over lunch about her boy's ear.
By two o'clock she'd booked him in at the clinic on the next street.
I don't need a page that tells me to replace anyone. My front desk is good.
I need to see what lunch and after six are costing me, and whether my desk gets an hour back.
If you put a robot face on it, I close the tab.

**Florence Nightingale: The Cost of Waiting**
Her method was to turn a column of figures into one picture that leaves no room to delay.
Here the column is missed calls, and the picture is money lost by month, stacked up over time.
The brief compares two ways to spend money. It leaves out the cost of spending nothing.
That third bar has to sit beside the other two, in the same units and on the same scale.
I'd add a 7-by-24 grid that shades the hours when calls go unanswered.

## Clash

**Brand strategist:** Clinic owner, here is my sketch. The ringing phone, five labelled inputs, then three bars, with "change nothing" in red. Can you draw anything simpler than that?

**Clinic owner:** Let me tell you about the last vendor. He showed me a demo where a voice said "press 1 for appointments", and my receptionist laughed out loud. So if your page says "automate" anywhere, I'm already gone. Call that bar "Cover the phone" and I'll keep reading.

**Luthier:** Then define "looked after" before we build anything. My proposal: the call is answered within three rings, and anything clinical goes to a staff member who calls back within 15 minutes. Those two numbers go on the page under the tool's bar.

**Florence Nightingale:** I've been arguing for the hour grid, and I'm dropping it now. It would need 168 inputs, and nobody fills in 168 boxes. One labelled field will do: "Busiest hour for missed calls." The picture still works with that.

**Brand strategist:** Then here's the shortcut, Florence Nightingale. Put a fourth bar next to the flat fee: the tool paid per booked appointment, $8 a booking. It uses the same inputs and shows the same bad case. If the calls dry up, the fee shrinks too.

**Clinic owner:** That's how my physio contractor works. He gets a share per session, and that's why he turns up on time. My accountant would forward that bar to me before I'd seen it.

**Luthier:** Brand strategist, here's the bad case in numbers. Missed calls halve from 40 to 20 a week, and 1 in 5 callers hangs up on the tool. That leaves 16 answered, 30% book, so 4.8 bookings a week, about 20.8 a month, at $180 each. Over 24 months that recovers $89,856. The tool on a flat fee costs $14,400. Per booking it costs $3,994. A hire at $4,200 a month fully loaded costs $100,800 and catches roughly the same bookings, so it ends about $11,000 short.

**Brand strategist:** Then the bold version holds and stays: "change nothing" is the most expensive bar. But we scale back one claim. The page says "up to" on staff time, and it doesn't promise the full figure.

**Florence Nightingale:** Clinic owner, I'd add one more labelled input: "Share of callers who hang up on a recorded voice," set to 20% by default. The bad case should be visible to the user, not buried in our assumptions.

**Clinic owner:** I'd rather you didn't. My old receptionist used to say that a number on a page becomes a promise. Put "hang up" in front of a nervous owner and it's the only thing they'll remember.

## Decision

The page asks a clinic owner for their missed calls, receptionist cost and tool price, then shows what hiring, covering the phone with a tool on a flat fee, covering it with a tool paid per booking, and changing nothing each cost at 6, 12 and 24 months.

Concept: Who Picks Up

- Brand strategist: the ringing-phone opening, and the four bars with "change nothing" in red and drawn to the same scale.
- Luthier: "Missed calls last week" as the first input, labels above every field in 16px, the definitions of "workload" and "looked after," and the email summary line at the end.
- Clinic owner: the name "Cover the phone" in place of "automate," the lunch and after-six framing, and the per-booking bar described in plain terms.
- Florence Nightingale: the "change nothing" bar as the anchor of the chart, and the single "Busiest hour for missed calls" field in place of the hour grid.
- Florence Nightingale lost the 168-cell grid because nobody would fill it in, and she said so herself. The hang-up input is still open between her and the clinic owner. The page ships with the 20% hang-up rate fixed in the bad-case toggle and no editable field, until a referee rules on it.

Bad case: missed calls halved to 20 a week and 1 in 5 callers hanging up. Over 24 months, both tool bars still recover far more than they cost ($89,856 recovered against $14,400 flat or $3,994 per booking). The hire bar ends about $11,000 short. The page holds, with staff time stated as "up to."

## Build notes

1. Build one HTML file with seven labelled inputs. Each label sits above its field and stays visible while typing:
   - Missed calls last week
   - How many months has this been happening
   - Receptionist salary per year
   - Weeks until a new hire answers alone
   - Average booking value
   - Tool monthly fee
   - Busiest hour for missed calls

   The two qualifying questions are missed calls and months. The result line multiplies them into "bookings lost since this started."
2. Draw four SVG bars at 6, 12 and 24 months on one shared y-axis: Hire, Cover the phone (flat), Cover the phone (per booking) and Change nothing. Add a "Bad case" toggle that halves call volume and applies the 20% hang-up rate to every bar at once.
3. Under the tool bars, print "Answered within 3 rings. Clinical calls passed to your staff, callback within 15 minutes. Your practice manager reviews call summaries and any billing each morning." End the page with a copyable one-line summary for an email.
